title: Graceful abort, chunk reclaimer and KV-lease notes
content:
Purpose
This note captures a compact, engineering-forward design for: graceful abort semantics in streaming generation, a chunk reclaimer (memory and KV lease model), and how those interact with scheduler backpressure and kernel preemption. The goal is to define behaviors that are safe for clients (no surprising deletes), efficient for the runtime (bounded memory/KV hold time), and compatible with rollouts/canaries.

Problem summary and motivation
We have three intersecting constraints: 1) clients may cancel requests mid-stream (explicit cancel or transport tear-down), 2) in-flight partial outputs occupy GPU memory, KV cache entries, and stream buffers, and 3) the serving scheduler needs to reclaim resources quickly to maintain latency SLOs and avoid head-of-line blocking. Current approaches either reclaim eagerly (risking visible inconsistency if client reconnects/resumes) or hold indefinitely (wastes resources). We need a middle path: a lease-based reclaim protocol with graceful abort that maintains idempotency guarantees for common patterns.

Key concepts and primitives
- Chunk: a contiguous sequence of generated tokens produced by a single model call that is either flushed to the client or held until flush.
- Partial token: a token or sub-token emitted but not acknowledged by client (e.g., streaming chunk sent but client closed the stream before server got ack).
- Lease (KV-lease): a server-side lease that pins KV cache entries / stream state for a short, bounded window after cancellation. Leases are lightweight epoch tokens attached to request IDs.
- Reclaimer: background routine that evicts chunk data and KV entries when lease expires, with hooks for metrics and optional pessimistic writeback.
- Graceful abort: cancellation semantics where the runtime emits a final termination token (internal) and holds minimal state for a deterministic resume window.

Behavioral requirements (client-facing invariants)
1) No silent corruption: if a client reconnects immediately with same request-id and can provide proof of last-seen token offset, the server should be able to resume or re-generate deterministically within the lease window.
2) Bound memory/kv exposure: resources held for canceled requests must be reclaimed within a configurable window (default 3s) unless policy escalates to long-term pin.
3) Observable cancellation: cancellations should appear in tracing and metrics (cancellation_reason, latency-to-evict, kv-lease-duration).
4) Idempotency compatibility: resume semantics should work with idempotent request ids and a checksum of the past prompt + model-version.

High-level protocol
1) Request lifecycle: request arrives with client-supplied idempotency_key (optional). Runtime assigns internal request_id and epoch. During generation the server streams chunks; each chunk has a chunk_id and sequence offset.
2) Client cancel path: client issues cancel or stream is closed. Server records cancel timestamp and transition to CANCELED state, emits an internal graceful-terminate signal to kernels to stop new decoding work for that request but to finish current micro-batch. A termination trace event is logged.
3) Lease issuance: on cancel, runtime issues a KV-lease with (request_id, epoch, expire_at = now + lease_window). Lease attaches lightweight refs to KV entries and to any disk-backed chunk buffers. Lease metadata is stored in the in-memory request table and replicated to watchers responsible for reclaimer tasks.
4) Reclaimer behavior: reclaimer scans expired leases and attempts eviction. If a request has no resume attempts and lease expired, reclaimer frees chunk buffers, deletes KV pins (or decrements refcount), and emits eviction metrics. If the request had cohort (canary rollout) hints or is marked for extended retention (debug flag), reclaimer may move buffers to a short-term cold store (compressed) instead of immediate delete.

Scheduler and kernel coordination
- Preemption: Graceful-terminate asks kernels to drain the current micro-batch immediately; kernels should not start new blocks for CANCELED requests. Kernel scheduling should prioritize occupant work as if it were low-cost to preempt, i.e., preemption cost recorded and used by scheduler heuristics to avoid frequent preempts.
- Backpressure signal: When request queues grow above threshold, scheduler should accelerate reclaimer heuristics (shrink lease window for new cancellations) and temporarily raise eviction priority for non-critical requests.
- Kernel-level KV eviction policy: kernels maintain local KV pin counts and accept lease API calls. When reclaimer evicts, kernels must ensure that ongoing attention caches are invalidated safely and that resumed requests will re-populate caches using the same model and quantization parameters.

Resume semantics and determinism
- Resume only allowed if: idempotency_key matches and checksum(prompt + model_metadata) matches, and resume attempt occurs before lease expiry. The client must supply last-acknowledged-token-offset. Server will attempt to resume from cached KV and chunk buffers; if cache is partially evicted, server will deterministically re-run the missing prefix decoding (bounded rework).
- If model or quantization changed since generation start, runtime should reject resume and return explicit 409 with reason "model-mismatch".

Partial-token atomicity and streaming semantics
- Token framing: To avoid half-token exposure across flaky transports (websockets HTTP/2 disconnects), the runtime emits tokens in framed atomic units where the smallest unit is a byte-range that the client must ack. Streaming transport layer will attempt best-effort ACK; if no ack, server treats final chunk as partially delivered and pins it under lease.
- Visible ordering: Reclaimer must not reorder chunks in resume path. Chunks store sequence offsets and a checksum. Resume logic verifies monotonic offsets before streaming resumed content.

Metrics, tracing and SLOs
- Key metrics: cancellations/sec, mean-lease-duration, evictions/sec, resumed/successful-resumes, rework-tokens-per-resume, avg-reclaim-latency.
- Tracing: include fields request_id, epoch, lease_id, cancel_ts, evict_ts, reclaim_reason. Span for kernel-preempt should include preempt-cost estimate.
- SLO knobs: default lease_window=3s (configurable per-customer), emergency-shrink-threshold for scheduler (queue depth percent), retain-debug-flag-window up to 5m for selected requests.

Failure modes and mitigations
- Lost lease metadata: if lease metadata lost (process crash) before reclaimer runs, a safe conservative fallback is to treat as expired and let the reclaimer on any replica evict; to avoid data-loss where resume requested, the resume will trigger full prefix re-generation.
- Repeat cancellations: frequent cancel/resume loops can overload scheduler; add per-key rate-limit and short cooldown.
- Partial KV eviction with inconsistent kernels: ensure eviction is only visible to resume path after a consistent barrier; prefer a two-phase release where kernels acknowledge release.

Operational runbook (short)
- Detect large spike in cancellations + high reclaim latency -> temporary increase lease_window to avoid churn + investigate upstream SDK bug.
- High resumed-rework-token metric -> indicates too-short lease or frequent model upgrades; increase lease_window for affected customer or pin model-version for generation.
- Debug trace: capture lease_id and kernel preempt spans; if missing, check watcher replication.

Open questions and decisions to make
- Default lease window tradeoffs: 3s vs 10s vs adaptive based on client RTT and model latency distribution. Proposal: adaptive by percentiles (p50 short, p99 longer) with per-customer overrides.
- Cold-store vs immediate free: do we compress and cold-store canceled buffers for 1-5 minutes for easier resume? Cost vs benefit depends on resume rate per customer; track per-customer resume frequency and decide.
- Should clients get a first-class resume API vs implicit idempotent re-call? Advantage of explicit API: simpler checks and clearer billing semantics. Drawback: more surface area.

Action items
- (A1) Implement lease metadata in request table + eviction watcher (Diego) — proto due in 2 wks.
- (A2) Scheduler flags to accelerate reclaim under queue pressure (Riley) — spike test plan assigned.
- (A3) Resume API proposal doc with examples and error codes (Priya) — draft for next sync.
- (A4) Add tracing fields and metrics in the streaming path (owner: Asha) — instrumentation PR.

Appendix: quick pseudocode for lease lifecycle
- on_cancel(request_id):
    lease_id = new_lease(request_id, expire=now + lease_window)
    attach_lease_to_kv(request_id, lease_id)
    emit_trace("lease_issued", lease_id)
- reclaimer_loop():
    for lease in expired_leases():
        if lease.has_resume_request_recently():
            extend_or_coldstore(lease)
        else:
            kernels.release_kv(lease.request_id, lease.lease_id)
            free_chunk_buffers(lease.request_id)
            emit_metric("eviction")

This doc is intentionally terse: it is meant as a working design to align infra, runtime, and kernel owners on the minimal viable lease semantics for safe, efficient cancellations and resumability. Comments welcome; flag items you think need a separate RFC (e.g., cross-region resume, long-term cold store costs).
